issues.legal_issue: The special statutory tenant category introduced by amendment applies only to tenants previously excluded by the former contractual exception, while the pre-existing tenant categories retain their distinct coverage.
material_facts: The tenants held written registered leases that included stipulations concerning the erection of buildings and constructed petrol-pump structures on the leased land.
The leases had expired, and the landlords sought recovery of possession.
The statutory amendments removed the former exception for leases with building stipulations and added a category for certain tenants previously denied statutory rights because of that exception.
issues.conclusion: The ordinary tenant categories cover tenants under oral or unregistered agreements, and tenants under registered agreements without a building stipulation, who satisfy the relevant statutory conditions. The added category applies only to tenants previously excluded from the Act by the former contractual exception; it does not impose new conditions on tenants already protected under the ordinary categories.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 2(4)(i), 2(4)(ii)(a), and 2(4)(ii)(b), read with Section 12, must be construed together with the retrospective amendments made in 1972 and 1973. The court applied the principle that statutory provisions should be read in their context and as a consistent whole, relying on Raghbir Singh Gill v. Gurcharan Singh Tohra and R v. Board of Trade. The added category was intended to extend protection to tenants formerly excluded by the Section 12 proviso, not to narrow existing protection.

predicates.tenant_claims_statutory_protection: A tenant seeks statutory protection in connection with a landlord's attempt to recover possession.
predicates.tenant_was_excluded_under_former_contrac: The tenant was formerly denied statutory protection because the lease contained a stipulation concerning the erection of buildings.

issues.definition: When a tenant seeks statutory protection and was formerly excluded because of a building stipulation in the lease, the added tenant category is limited to tenants previously excluded on that basis.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant who has constructed a building on leased land but is not in actual physical possession of it is not entitled to the statutory protection claimed in an ejectment proceeding.
material_facts: The oil companies had taken land on long-term leases, constructed petrol pumps, and allowed appointed dealers to operate them under dealership agreements.
The leases had expired, the landlords sought possession, and the companies applied for statutory protection and an order for sale of the land.
The companies were not in actual physical possession of the premises occupied by the dealers or other third parties.
issues.conclusion: The companies were not entitled to the Act's protection and benefits because they were not in actual physical possession of the buildings; the appeals were dismissed and the High Court orders were upheld.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 2(4) and 9, read with the Act's purpose of protecting tenants who occupy and use their buildings, require actual physical possession for the relevant protection in these circumstances. The court applied its earlier ruling in Bharat Petroleum Corporation Ltd. v. Nirmala that the phrase “actual physical possession” requires factual, not merely legal or deemed, possession; that ruling operated as res judicata for parties to that case and as binding precedent under Article 141 for other cases. It also relied on P. Ananthakrishnan Nair v. Dr. G. Ramakrishnan and S.R. Radhakrishnan v. Neelamegam on the protective purpose of Section 9 and the tenant's need to occupy the premises.

predicates.tenant_seeks_protection_in_ejectment_pro: A tenant seeks statutory protection while the landlord is pursuing an ejectment or possession proceeding.
predicates.tenant_constructed_building: The tenant constructed a building on the leased land.
predicates.tenant_in_actual_physical_possession: The tenant physically occupies the building rather than having possession held by a third party.

issues.definition: In an ejectment proceeding, a tenant who constructed a building but does not physically occupy it is not entitled to the statutory protection at issue.

issues.legal_issue: The statutory tenant definition includes qualifying heirs but excludes subtenants and their heirs.
material_facts: The statutory definition separately included heirs of tenants in specified protected categories and expressly excluded subtenants and their heirs.
The companies' buildings were operated by dealers or other third parties, and the companies sought the protections available to tenants.
issues.conclusion: Heirs of tenants within the specified protected categories may receive the Act's benefits, but subtenants and their heirs are excluded from those benefits, including the right to seek purchase of the land and compensation under the Act.
issues.legal_principle: Section 2(4)(ii)(c) includes heirs of persons described in Section 2(4)(i), Section 2(4)(ii)(a), or Section 2(4)(ii)(b), while expressly excluding subtenants and their heirs. The court read that express exclusion to apply to rights under the Act, including the rights under Sections 3 and 9.

predicates.claimant_seeks_statutory_tenant_protecti: A claimant seeks benefits available to a tenant under the statutory scheme.
predicates.claimant_is_heir_of_covered_tenant: The claimant is an heir of a tenant within one of the protected statutory categories.
predicates.claimant_is_subtenant_or_subtenant_heir: The claimant is a subtenant or an heir of a subtenant.

issues.definition: A claimant seeking statutory tenant protection is eligible as an heir only if the claimant inherits from a tenant in a protected category; subtenants and their heirs are excluded.
